Q: Why gcc linker change the assembly instructions? A:

The push 0x0(%rip) in your object file has a relocation entry. During linking, the linker recognises it can optimise this into a direct call instruction instead.

The addr32 prefix is added because the call target requires a 32-bit addressing.

Why only some Machines?

Different linker versions, flags or library configurations (static or dynamic) can affect this optimisation

Is this causing your crash?

The transformation itself is valid. Your crash is likely from:

  1. Stack alignment issues: the push added 8 bytes; the call doesn't

  2. Calling convention problems: if surrounding code expected that push

Try Debugging this:

#check the relocation at offset 0x89b
objdump -r your_object.o | grep 89b

#Try disabling relaxation
gcc -Wl, --no-relax ...

Q: Are Void and () isomorphic in the presence of laziness? A:

No, they are not equivalent. What your linked comment and answer are saying is something different: they are saying that different people have different opinions on how to think about undefined in a lazy setting. Some folks will consider Void to have zero possible values and () to have one, because there are no constructors for Void and one constructor (with no fields) for (); meanwhile, other folks will consider Void to have one possible value and () to have two, because undefined is a possible value of either type. These two types of folks don't disagree on any important facts; they only disagree on what kinds of things are interesting/useful to think about. But if you want to cater to both types of people, then you must discuss both ways of thinking when trying to add a field to a data type without changing its meaning -- because the word "meaning" itself has a different meaning to the two types of people.

In fact, it's somewhat common for a single person to hold both points of view! In different contexts, one or the other view is more useful or clear, and it's relatively common to code switch between the two ways of talking about the world.

Q: Merging the headers then concatenate the records of a huge number of text files A:

I get a significant speedup by using tail instead of awk for the final catenation using 16 copies of a 635MB testfile:

$ wget -O test.vcf.gz https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/toolbox/gbench/samples/vcf/GCA_000001215.4_current_ids.vcf.gz
$ gunzip test.vcf.gz
$ seq 16 | xargs -I@ awk '
    !/^#/{
      printf "%s\0",FILENAME >>"names"
      printf "+%d\0%s\0",FNR+1,FILENAME >>"offsets"
      nextfile
    } 1' test.vcf |
  awk '!seen[$0]++ && /^##/; END{print}' > header
$ time <names xargs -0 awk '!/^#/' >/dev/null

real    1m0.178s
user    0m54.389s
sys 0m5.787s
$ time <offsets xargs -0 -n2 tail -n >/dev/null

real    0m8.464s
user    0m3.318s
sys 0m5.142s

but this test is CPU-bound. Since your bottleneck is probably I/O to storage, your difference may be less.
